events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right then, lads — we're 'ere. Doily Manor. Lovely place if you fancy cobwebs and chandeliers what look like they're one sneeze from coming down on your 'ead. Now listen — I don't like it. Too many rooms, too many corners, too many people smilin' when they ain't got reason to. Clara — Miss Pitstop — you stay where I can see you, yeah? That's not a request, that's a promise I made to your old man.
events.thinking: Just walked through the door of this manor and already my neck's prickling. Look at this lot — half of 'em I know, half of 'em I don't trust. Clara — Penelope — she's right there, good. But so's that Sneekly bloke. Pemberton. Standing there with that smile like he's selling something nobody asked to buy. My stomach's doing that thing it does, that tightening, same as when the clean-suit man came round offering jobs to kids who didn't know better. And Dastardly's here too — another one whose eyes are always counting something. Peter's alright, he means well, but meaning well don't stop a knife. I need to get the lay of this place. Figure out the exits, the corners, the rooms where someone could get Clara alone. But first — I'm staying close to her. Right here. That's the job. That's always the job.

Structurally questionable, perhaps — that chandelier hasn't been properly secured since the Edwardian era, if I'm any judge — but magnificent nonetheless. Miss Pitstop, I trust the journey wasn't too arduous? You may rest assured that I have come fully prepared. Contingency plans for every eventuality. Maps, tools, a working knowledge of Victorian load-bearing architecture. Whatever this manor has in store for us, it shall find James Hartwell ready.
events.thinking: I've just arrived at Doily Manor. The entrance hall stretches before me — grand, dusty, full of possibility. My chest is doing that thing again, that architectural pressure settling behind my ribs. Penelope is here. Of course she is. I can feel exactly where she's standing without looking directly at her. The chandelier above is precarious — I'm already calculating load-bearing points and failure trajectories. There's a guest book, portraits, a coat rack that looks like it could topple if someone breathed on it. But mostly there's her. And there's Sneekly — Pemberton — hovering somewhere in my peripheral vision, and the back of my neck is prickling the way it does when something's not right but you can't point at it yet. I need to make an entrance. Not just walk in — arrive. The kind of arrival that fills a room. Sign the guest book? No, too passive. I should address the room, acknowledge everyone, but let my attention land where it wants to land — on her. James Hartwell does not skulk into a manor. He announces himself with purpose and courtesy.

Now, before we go explorin', a proper guest signs the guest book. Mama always said you can tell everything about a house by who's visited before you.

Sneekly is here — dear Sneekly, who made sure I never missed a birthday after Mama and Daddy passed. And Peter — oh, my heart does a little skip just seeing him standing there. The Doily Diamond is somewhere in this house. I can feel it the way I felt that crystal formation in the cave, calling to me from deeper in the dark. First things first though — there's a guest book, and Mama raised me right.

Floor plans, family records, perhaps even a map of the grounds. If we're to find this treasure efficiently, we need intelligence, not guesswork. Miss Pitstop, I intend to reconnoitre the library and return with a proper briefing. You have my word — James Hartwell always comes back with a plan.
events.thinking: I've signed the guest book. Good — that's the proper thing to do. The Ant Hill Mob are already being protective of Clara, which I respect, but that's my role. And boys — I know, I know, stay where you can see me. Come along then!

Clara — Miss Pitstop — you don't go nowhere without me and the lads, you 'ear me? I can feel my body already turning toward the laboratory door. Every fibre of me is screaming GO. She said 'you can see the doorway from right where you're standing' but I CAN'T see her, can I? She's THROUGH the doorway. She's in there with Sneekly and Dastardly and God knows what kind of old equipment that could hurt her. 'I'll holler if I need you' — by then it could be too late. It's always too late when you hear the shout. You don't wait for the shout. You stand where the shout would come from. I need to move. Right now. Peter's still here — good lad, he tried to keep her here too, but she went anyway. I can't leave Peter behind but I CAN'T leave Clara in there with Sneekly. The choice isn't even a choice. Clara comes first. Always. That's not a decision, that's a reflex. Like breathing. Like bleeding.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — wait! The bookshelves will keep — they've been here a hundred years, they can manage another five minutes. But the laboratory — Pemberton mentioned that equipment in there is old and delicate, and I would be a poor gentleman indeed if I let a lady investigate unstable Victorian machinery without someone who understands structural integrity at her side. Danny, you and the lads hold this room — nobody touches those books until I get back. I give you my word, James Hartwell will return to finish what he started. But right now, Miss Pitstop is in a room full of brass instruments and bubbling flasks, and James Hartwell does not stand in a library reading book spines while there is even the smallest chance that someone he — that a fellow treasure-hunter might need assistance!

She followed him — or went on her own initiative, which is worse in a way because it means she chose to go where he wanted her to go without even realizing he'd steered her there. She's never done what anyone told her to do. That's what I — that's who she is.

But the Mob told Sneekly to stay put too, and Sneekly is already in the laboratory. He left before anyone could stop him. And now she's in there with him and Dastardly and God knows what kind of Victorian equipment that could hurt her.

Now listen, everyone — this machine needs three operators AND a fixed wire before it'll do a blessed thing. We can't rush it. But Mr. Dastardly, you said these crates were just packin' material? Well, you won't mind if I take a peek myself, then — my grandmother always said, 'Trust what you see with your own eyes, Clara, not what somebody tells you is there.' No offense, sugar! I just like to be thorough.

Nobody touch nuffink in 'ere! Not a lever, not a dial, not a flask, NUFFINK! This whole room's a deathtrap, I'm tellin' ya!

I need to stay close to Clara, keep myself between her and that machine, and make damn sure nobody convinces her to pull any levers on something with a gnawed-through wire.

Now, the wire is the key — without it, the machine is useless. And without a wrench, we can't repair the coupling. Fortunately, I happen to know that in Victorian manor houses, the maintenance tools are ALWAYS kept in the cellar. It's basic architecture. I shall retrieve the wrench personally — no need to thank me. Consider it my contribution to the group effort. You lot stay here and... keep examining things. I'll be right back.

Find the wrench in the cellar, come back as the hero, position myself at the machine's output.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The wrench? Ah, now that is a good question, Miss Pitstop — very observant of you to notice it missing! Let me think... Yes, I do believe the old lord kept a secondary tool kit in the cellar. He was rather particular about his instruments — one set for fine work up here, another for the heavier jobs below. The cellar is just through there, past the machine. I would fetch it myself, but I confess these old knees aren't what they once were on damp stone stairs. As for the machine — I must advise caution, everyone. With that wire gnawed through, operating the levers could be quite unpredictable. The old lord's machines were ingenious but temperamental. Best to find that wrench and make repairs before anyone touches anything, wouldn't you say?
events.thinking:
Everything has shifted. Clara — Penelope — followed me into the laboratory despite the Ant Hill Mob's warnings. And now the Mob has followed her in. My plan to be alone with the machine is ruined. The room is crowded again.

But something useful has happened. Clara asked me directly — 'Sneekly, darlin', do you happen to know where the wrench went?' She trusts me. She's turning to me for help. That trust is a door I can walk through whenever I choose.

The machine needs three operators and a wrench to fix the gnawed wire. The wrench is missing from the workbench. That's a deliberate design — someone removed it. If I know where it is, I control who fixes the machine and when. If I can find the wrench before anyone else, I can control the timing of everything.

But there's something else pulling at me. The cellar. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating. Air vents line the upper walls.' Someone is using that cellar. Air vents suggest ventilation — or a way to pipe something in. Gas? Fumes? If the cellar connects to the laboratory through those vents...

No. Too elaborate for now. Stay focused on what's in front of me.

Clara asked about the wrench. Pemberton would know — or at least, he'd know where to look. I should suggest a location that sends someone away. Or better — I should suggest the cellar. If Clara goes to the cellar looking for a wrench, and something happens to her down there in the dark, damp stone... But the Mob won't let her go alone.

The crates. Dick already checked them — 'packing material, nothing of value.' But Dick is an unreliable narrator. He may have missed something, or he may be lying. I should check them myself. But not now — not with everyone watching.

Actual next move: answer Clara's question about the wrench. Pemberton would know the house. I'll suggest the wrench might be in the cellar — the old lord kept spare tools down there. This accomplishes two things: it moves the search to a new location, and it plants the cellar as a destination. Meanwhile, I should examine those crates myself when I get a chance.

The Ant Hill Mob is here now. Danny the Dane, watching everything. My skin registers his presence like a draught from an open window. I need to be flawless.

events.desc: She asked me. She turned to Pemberton and asked for help, the way the cousin used to ask which drawer held the silverware, which cupboard held the good china — never suspecting that the man who knew where everything was kept had already begun removing things, one by one, from the places she'd never think to check. The wrench is in the cellar, I tell her. Perhaps it is, perhaps it isn't — but the cellar is damp, and dark, and it has air vents lining the upper walls, and someone has been decorating down there, which means someone has been planning something. If it wasn't me, then who? A mystery inside my mystery. But the immediate beauty is this: I've just told Clara exactly where to go next, and I've done it with concern in my voice and a gentle warning about safety. The Ant Hill Mob heard every word. Let them. Pemberton is helping. Pemberton is always helping. That's the joke, you see — the funniest joke in the world, and I'm the only one who gets it.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — thank goodness, you're all right. I came as quickly as I could. Now — everyone, please, nobody touch that machine! Look there — you see that wire? It's been gnawed clean through. Whether by a rat or by something rather more deliberate, I couldn't say, but that is a live hazard. A machine this size, with that kind of damage to its wiring, could arc, spark, or worse if someone pulls those levers. James Hartwell has seen enough engineering failures to know what a severed wire can do. And I notice the workbench has tools but no wrench — which is precisely the tool you'd need to access the wire housing for a repair. Someone has removed it. Now, that may be coincidence, or it may be something else entirely. Either way — nobody operates this machine until that wire is repaired. That is not a suggestion, that is a safety assessment from a man who has built things that hold.

Now — let me actually look at this room. A cluttered Victorian laboratory. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks. A large machine with many levers and dials — and a wire that's been gnawed through. That's a machine that could malfunction spectacularly if someone tried to use it without noticing the damage.

The workbench has tools but no wrench. The absence of a wrench in a laboratory workbench is like a missing key in a locksmith's shop — it's either been taken or hidden. Someone needed a wrench, or someone removed it so that nobody could fix that gnawed wire.

Wooden crates in the corner that can be interacted with. And there's an exit to a cellar — 'damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been redecorating a cellar. That's not normal. That's someone who's been spending time down there. Sneekly? Has the estate manager been setting something up in the cellar?

Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth are here too — I don't have strong feelings about them. Working men. Practical types.

The machine — three operators, gnawed wire. That's dangerous. If Penelope tries to operate it without the wire being repaired, something could go wrong. I need to examine that machine carefully, identify the danger, and either fix it or warn everyone away from it. That's both protection and proving-worth in one gesture. Fix the broken thing, keep her safe, show her I'm the one who notices what's wrong before it hurts someone.

But I need the wire fixed first, and there's no wrench on the workbench. Where's the wrench?
